14.0.s.en: (1) Receiving the one who is weak in faith

14.0.0.en: After St. Paul laid down the foundations of faith among Christians of Jewish origin and of Gentile origin, here he solves a secondary problem in order to put an end to every division in the Church. He found that there were two groups: one he called the weak in faith, who are mostly Christians of Jewish origin, influenced by their former worship in that they did not eat certain foods such as pork, considering them unclean for them. He called them weak in faith because they were still bound by the letter of the Law with a measure of scrupulosity. He commanded that no one from the second group, who eat everything with thanksgiving, should despise them, and also that the weak in faith should not judge the strong in faith for eating everything, for God has received both groups as they are.

14.1.0.en: Then he addresses both groups, that neither should judge the other, because they are both servants of God, and God alone is responsible for each one, since He receives each one and establishes each one in Him, for He is able to do so.

14.1.1.en: Pay attention, beloved, to your discussions, for how much of your time and the time of others have you wasted in foolish debates, arguments and inquiries whose aim is to prove yourself and that please Christ in no way, but make you fall into much judging.

14.2.0.en: Some Christians of Jewish origin held fast to the feasts of the Jews at the beginning of Christianity, and these have spiritual meanings, such as the Day of Atonement, that is, the redemption of Christ, and the Feast of Tabernacles, which means the world's being a place of exile, and so on. The other group, that is, the Christians of Gentile origin and the rest of those of Jewish origin, lived these meanings every day, because the Christian feasts had not yet been fixed at the beginning of the apostolic age, except the feast of the Resurrection. Likewise the first group did not eat certain foods forbidden among the Jews, while the other group ate everything with thanksgiving for God's sake. So the Apostle Paul asks all of them that neither should judge the other, for the purpose of all is good, which is drawing near to God.

14.3.0.en: What matters is that a person lives to please God by good works and not himself, that is, his personal opinions, and even if he dies, he dies in the faith, pleasing God. He made clear that God accepts differences between individuals, if the purpose is to please God, but calmly. In this he protects the Church from individualistic tendencies that could lead to the division of the Church, if they are tied to pride and to not submitting to her teachings and guidance.

14.4.0.en: Life, in all its details, for the believer is nothing but an offering of the love of God, in which he tries, as much as he can, with the capabilities and energies he has been given, to please God and be faithful in his talents. The Christian is strong; he does not fear death but welcomes it, since it is his goal, because it will lead to seeing Christ in heaven.

14.5.0.en: The plan and design of the Lord Christ, when He died, rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, was to reign by love over the hearts of the believers on earth and of those who have triumphed in heaven.

14.6.0.en: St. Paul returns, saying to the group weak in faith, "Do not judge your brother," and saying to the group strong in faith, "Do not despise the actions of the one weak in faith," but let each one turn to himself, rebuking himself for his own sins, because every person of every race or religion will bow and stand before the throne of Christ, giving an account of himself and his own works, not the works of his brother.

14.6.1.en: Judging distracts you from your repentance, so examine yourself every day and begin spiritual striving, and through the labors of striving you will feel the weakness of others and their need for your prayer instead of judging.

14.7.s.en: (2) Do not cause the weak in faith to stumble

14.7.0.en: Instead of despising the weak, let our chief concern be not to cause him to stumble by our eating things unclean in his sight, knowing that there is no unclean food in God's sight, but it is unclean only from the viewpoint of the one who counts it unclean, that is, in the sight of the one weak in faith.

14.8.0.en: "Grieved": stumbled. If the law of love for the other is the highest of the Church's laws, then we must not insist on eating or doing things that grieve your weak brother, who is precious in God's sight because Christ died for him. So for God's sake do not eat in front of him and do not cause him to stumble, lest he doubt you and think you sinful, saying that you are not righteous and that you violate the commandments of God, though in truth you are righteous and live in the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

14.8.1.en: If you are connected with the Church or serve in it, you must care for those who are far away, and not do in front of them things that they could misunderstand and so be caused to stumble because of you, because you are a model and example for them, and they do not expect error from you and seek to be like you as an angel. Likewise parents should be mindful of their conduct in front of their children; their anger and quarreling, for example, is very distressing to the children.

14.9.0.en: Because the Kingdom of God, which is within us and which we live with Christ, is essentially love, joy and peace, it is not right for us to be occupied with discussions or stumblings concerning eating and drinking. Has not the Church arranged long fasts throughout the year to protect us from preoccupation with food and to give us more heavenly things?

14.10.0.en: "These things": love, joy and peace. Let our first aim then be to please Christ by making love and peace, and in this also people will commend us, that is, praise us, so that we become a good example that gladdens them and not a stumbling block from which they recoil.

14.11.0.en: So it is good that we not squander our energies on what does not benefit the Church, but work and watch with all diligence to establish peace among the members of the Church and prevent divisions. Let all our speech be not for tearing down the other and proving our point of view right, but let us speak spiritual words that build him up spiritually and make him grow in Christ, for "he that winneth souls is wise" (Prov 11:30).

14.12.0.en: The work of God, which is the salvation of souls and their spiritual edification, is far more important than food. It is not right to destroy the work of God so that you may eat in your freedom and cause your brother to stumble, because this conduct would be evil on your part and you would become evil in the sight of God.

14.13.0.en: It is better for you not to eat meat nor drink wine, nor anything that could cause your brother to stumble.

14.14.0.en: You will say to me, "But I believe that this food is not unclean." Well, then eat it, but not in front of people weak in faith, only by yourself before God, and then your conscience will be at rest and will not condemn you in the eating that you consider good and not unclean.

14.15.0.en: But the one who eats something while doubting and not confident in the rightness of what he does, it is better that he not eat it, lest sin be counted against him.

14.15.1.en: Our love for others, and Paul's longing and praise for the Romans

15.0.s.en: (1) The strong in faith is the one who bears with the other

15.0.0.en: St. Paul begins his chapter with a verse that sums up the previous chapter, which is that the one who is strong in his faith and in his love for God gives up what comforts and pleases himself so as not to burden the one weak in faith, and even bears with long-suffering and takes in with a wide heart the thoughts and opinions of those weak in faith. This is contrary to the thinking of the world, which supposes that the one who bears with others is a weak person without personality.

15.0.1.en: This is fulfilled in practice when the servant, or parents, humble themselves before the one served or the children, listening to their opinions calmly and with love without attacking them or silencing them with big words, and in time they will find the opportunity to correct some wrong concepts calmly.

15.1.0.en: So let each one think how he will win the other without selfishness. But to what extent should I please the other? The deciding factor is the good and righteousness, meaning that servants accept the opinions of the one served or the opinions of the other as long as they do not conflict with what is good and right, and it is never required that the Church concede, be lax and become careless about concepts that may lead the one served to destruction, or else the Church would lose her holiness, become like the world, and lose the one served forever as well.

15.2.0.en: Although the world today teaches a person to live pleasing himself with extreme selfishness even if the other is harmed, the Lord Christ did not teach us this, but looked to what pleases us, that is, salvation and redemption, and bore sufferings and insults for our sake, so that He cried out to the Father, saying, all the insults that those who reject You want to say to You have insulted Me with while I am crucified on the Cross.

15.3.0.en: The previous verse and all the verses of the Old Testament were written not as history, but so that we may learn how to walk spiritually by suffering for the sake of others. For the word of God written in the Holy Bible comforts us and gives us patience in our sufferings, so that we can bear the sufferings of the present in the hope that our labors will turn to glory in the end.

15.4.0.en: God promises to support His children with patience and inner comfort, so that they continue in their love for all and in seeking their salvation.

15.4.1.en: For the one who pleases another at his own expense, God opens to him unlimited energies and countless compensations, and even patience itself becomes easy. How many times have we heard in the rich history of our Church of saints who bore with others with patience and joy.

15.5.0.en: "One mind": feelings of love that bring all together.

15.5.1.en: "One mouth": one thought and one teaching.

15.5.2.en: In this you are rid of division in the Church, and you become one mind and one mouth, and thus the name of Christ is glorified when the world sees His children as one unity without division.

15.6.0.en: If the holy, perfect Christ received us, defiled sinners, despite the vast difference between us and Him, how much more should we, weak sinful human beings, receive our weak brothers with love, whatever their condition or mistakes.

15.6.1.en: Do not forget your one goal, which is the salvation of yourself and others. Give up your comfort and desires to win those around you. For in the midst of our selfish world, the love that everyone needs shines forth. Offer your love, even with a smile or a small word of encouragement, and pray for all.

15.7.s.en: (2) Receiving the Jews and the Gentiles

15.7.1.en: The Jews and the Gentiles are equal in that Christ served both by offering them salvation, not because of any merit in them. He saved the Jews because of His promise to their fathers that He would save their descendants despite their many disobediences, and as for the Gentiles, the prophecies (Ps 18:49) and (Deut 32:43), which St. Paul cites in (vv. 9, 10) respectively, had already indicated that God would have mercy on them because He is a God of love, mercy and compassion, even though they were unworthy because of their many sins.

15.8.0.en: "A root of Jesse": the Lord Christ. "To reign over": your King.

15.8.1.en: He also affirms the joy of the Gentiles because God saved them, as it came in (Ps 117:1). Not only that, but the Lord Christ will be your King (Isa 11:10), that is, He will reign over your hearts and thoughts, and the state of enmity between you and Him will end and turn into hope in Him, that is, confidence that He loves you and saves you. He specified the Gentiles in the two verses (vv. 11, 12), to erase from their hearts any sense of inferiority in comparison with the Jews.

15.8.2.en: Among the greatness of God's mercy is that every person is placed in God's plan of salvation, even those far away who were not given the opportunity of spiritual teaching in their youth. A day will come when the grace and work of God visits them with power, and has mercy on them and brings them back to His embrace if they wish. So take care to show Christ to those far away, invite them to the Church and pray for them however evident their evil, for God seeks their salvation and is able to turn them into saints.

15.9.0.en: Finally St. Paul prays for them that the grace of the Holy Spirit may support them, so that they may stand firm and their hope and certainty in Christ increase, and they rejoice in their life with God and feel peace.

15.10.0.en: In humility, the Apostle Paul praises the Romans so that they would not think that he is being harsh with them and counts them sinners, but he makes clear that in his eyes they have reached a high level of goodness and knowledge, and that among them are people of a high degree of holiness, who are able to counsel and rebuke the wrongdoers among the Romans for their salvation.

15.11.0.en: "The more boldly": Paul dared and spoke of new depths in the faith, since he saw that the level of faith of the believers in Rome could bear this deep speech.

15.11.1.en: "In some sort": in some parts of the epistle.

15.11.2.en: Why then did the Apostle write to them?

15.11.3.en: To remind them of some truths of the faith, and this is a gentle and humble approach from Paul, to regard his words as a mere reminder to them because they know everything.

15.12.0.en: This perfection makes them without blemish. Then he said that only here can I, Paul, the minister to the Gentiles, stand before Jesus Christ like the priest who offers sacrifices. But instead of offering a holy offering of fine flour and without blemish, I offer you to God, since your heart, your mind and your life have been sanctified by the Holy Spirit and have become worthy to be offered to God like the offering without blemish.

15.13.0.en: When I say that I am the minister to the Gentiles, do not think that I am boasting of myself, for all the glory and boasting goes back to Christ Jesus, who strengthened me for the ministry to the Gentiles, which became my portion by the plan of the Father.

15.14.0.en: I do not dare to attribute the credit to myself, because all the credit goes back to the work of Christ in my words and deeds, so that the Gentiles might return to obeying God.

15.15.0.en: "Illyricum": northwest of Macedonia, in present-day Greece.

15.15.1.en: Christ performed miracles and wonders through me, the weak one, by the power of His Holy Spirit, so that God was able to work through my weakness and bring the Gospel to the region lying between Jerusalem and Illyricum.

15.15.2.en: Note, beloved, that the more the servant humbles himself and feels his weakness, the more God works through him many powers and wonders. So thank God after every work you do, and ask His help before everything.

15.16.0.en: "Christ was named": Christ had been preached.

15.16.1.en: "Another man's foundation": one of the apostles who had preached in a place and founded a church there.

15.16.2.en: I was careful to preach in regions where the Gospel had not reached before by another apostle, so as not to rob the other apostles of their rights. For each apostle has a region in which to preach and reap its fruit. This is precision and humility on Paul's part in respecting the feelings of the other apostles, but it is not wrong for two apostles to preach in one place.

15.16.3.en: Although cooperation among servants is beneficial and necessary, on the other hand let each servant have his own ministry on which he concentrates, lest he trouble the other with his interference. So look for the neglected ministry or the souls far away, and do not run after ministries that are visible and praised by others out of love of appearing.

15.17.0.en: The Apostle Paul acknowledges that he preached in places that had not heard of Christ before, and by this they saw and heard of Christ, in fulfillment of the prophecy of Isaiah (Isa 52:15).

15.18.0.en: Paul wished many times to visit Rome, but each time he was hindered from visiting them, but now, since he has finished preaching in and visiting the regions he intended in his plan, nothing remains but Rome to visit. Therefore he will come to them, and after he is filled with them in part, he will set out to Spain, since he will never be filled with them.

15.19.0.en: Before Paul comes to Rome, he will first go to Jerusalem to minister to the needy believers, since contributions have been collected from the regions of Macedonia and Achaia, which are Gentile cities, to be given to the people of Jerusalem, and this is love and generosity on their part. But from his viewpoint this is considered a return of favor, for just as the Jews shared their spiritual things with the Gentiles, so the Gentiles share with them in material needs.

15.20.0.en: When he has finished this offering, which is the fruit of the Gentiles' love for the Jews, he will pass by them on his way to Spain.

15.21.0.en: When he comes to them he will find them at a high degree of spiritual life filled with blessing, since they will have left their divisions and trained in acts of love and in receiving the other.

15.22.0.en: In humility and need he asks them to pray for him and with him diligently and persistently, because he is about to face a hard trial, which is confronting the unbelieving Jews in Jerusalem, who will devise plots against him, and this is what actually happened afterward. And he asks for prayer not in order to escape hardships, for hardships do not matter to him, but he prays that the ministry, which is the desire of his heart, may succeed, and that the people of Jerusalem may accept the offering of love presented by the Gentiles.

15.22.1.en: Therefore the Church always prays for her shepherds, the Patriarch, the bishops, the priests and the servants, that the Lord may complete their ministry.

15.23.0.en: In this my heart rejoices at the completion of the ministry and at meeting you, which I longed for.

15.24.0.en: Finally he prays for them that God may be with them in all matters of their life, He who is the King of peace, the Giver of peace to all who follow Him.

15.24.1.en: Take care to offer love to everyone in need, so that you become accustomed to doing good, and even long to meet every person to give him your love. Then the love of God and His mercy will overflow upon you, and your giving will increase until your whole life becomes love for everyone.

15.24.2.en: Greetings from Paul and his companions to the believers in Rome, and a warning against false teachers
